best_for: Windows users who live in PowerShell, Command Prompt or WSL and want tabs, split panes and their own key shortcuts in one window.

points.title: One window for every shell
points.text: Any command-line program can be a profile: PowerShell, Command Prompt, Azure Cloud Shell or a WSL distribution such as Ubuntu. Profiles for WSL and extra PowerShell versions appear on their own.

points.title: Tabs and panes
points.text: Open tabs with Ctrl+Shift+T, split panes with Alt+Shift+D, and drag a tab out into its own window. The `wt` command can open a whole layout of tabs and panes from a script.

points.title: Set it as the default
points.text: On Windows 11, and on Windows 10 22H2 after the May 2023 update, you can make it the default terminal, so every console program opens inside it.

points.title: Settings in a screen or a file
points.text: Most options sit in a settings screen; the rest live in `settings.json`, which you can open by holding Shift while choosing Settings. Color schemes, fonts, backgrounds and every shortcut can be changed.

points.title: No auto-update outside the Store
points.text: Builds from the Store update themselves. Builds installed from GitHub do not, so you update them by hand or through winget. A separate Preview edition carries features before they reach stable.

points.title: Windows only, per user
points.text: There is no Mac or Linux version. The MSIX packages listed here install per user, cover x86, x64 and Arm64, and need Windows 10 version 2004 (build 19041) or later. The Windows listing keeps 68 versions, and the app is open source under MIT.
